title: What is the difference between an effectively final variable and an explicitly final variable when captured by a lambda (none — the compiler treats them identically; both are legal to capture; final just makes the restriction explicit)?

s1_definition.profdef: There is NO difference in behavior. A variable is "effectively final" if it is never reassigned after initialization — the compiler treats it IDENTICALLY to an explicitly `final` variable for lambda capture purposes. Both can be captured by lambdas. Both produce the same bytecode. The only difference is style: `final` makes the immutability CONTRACT visible in the source code (self-documenting), while effectively final relies on the compiler's analysis. Java 8 relaxed the rule: before Java 8, anonymous inner classes required explicitly `final`; Java 8 lambdas accept effectively final — `final` keyword became optional.
s1_definition.analogy: Two bank employees follow the same rule: "never change the interest rate during a transaction." Employee A has a SIGNED POLICY (explicitly final) — the rule is written on paper. Employee B just naturally never changes the rate (effectively final) — no paper, same behavior. The bank (compiler) trusts both equally. The paper just makes it obvious to OTHER employees (readers) that the rate won't change.
s1_definition.oneliner: Effectively final = never reassigned (compiler checks). Explicitly final = `final` keyword (you declare). Both identical for lambda capture. `final` is documentation, not a different rule.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** There is NO difference in behavior. A variable is "effectively final" if it is never reassigned after initialization — the compiler treats it IDENTICALLY to an explicitly `final` variable for lambda capture purposes. Both can be captured by lambdas. Both produce the same bytecode. The only difference is style: `final` makes the immutability CONTRACT visible in the source code (self-documenting), while effectively final relies on the compiler's analysis. Java 8 relaxed the rule: before Java 8, anonymous inner classes required explicitly `final`; Java 8 lambdas accept effectively final — `final` keyword became optional.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Two bank employees follow the same rule: "never change the interest rate during a transaction." Employee A has a SIGNED POLICY (explicitly final) — the rule is written on paper. Employee B just naturally never changes the rate (effectively final) — no paper, same behavior. The bank (compiler) trusts both equally. The paper just makes it obvious to OTHER employees (readers) that the rate won't change.

**One line to remember:** Effectively final = never reassigned (compiler checks). Explicitly final = `final` keyword (you declare). Both identical for lambda capture. `final` is documentation, not a different rule.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's code review found inconsistency:** some developers use `final` on every captured variable, others rely on effectively final. A junior developer thought removing `final` would break the lambda — it didn't. The team creates a demonstration showing that both behave identically, the reassignment error location differs, and when explicit `final` adds documentation value (method parameters, configuration, captured loop variables).

**What the project will show:** Side-by-side explicitly final vs effectively final capture, identical behavior proof, reassignment error location difference, when `final` is valuable as documentation, and the Java 7 vs Java 8 history (anonymous class required final, lambda accepts effectively final).

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** `final BigDecimal threshold = 200000` and `BigDecimal threshold = 200000` (never reassigned). Both capture the value 200000 in the lambda.

**Step 2.** Lambda `t -> t.amount().compareTo(threshold) > 0` executes identically in both cases. Same bytecode. Same captured value. Same result: TRD-001, TRD-003, TRD-005 (amounts > 200000).

**Step 3.** If you add `threshold = 300000` AFTER the effectively final declaration: compile error AT THE LAMBDA line ("must be final or effectively final"). If you add it after the explicit `final` declaration: compile error AT THE ASSIGNMENT line ("cannot assign to final"). Different error location, same protection.

```
  EXPLICITLY FINAL:
    final BigDecimal threshold = 200000;
    threshold = 300000;  // ERROR HERE: "cannot assign to final variable"
    Lambda captures threshold (Recommended) 

  EFFECTIVELY FINAL:
    BigDecimal threshold = 200000;
    // never reassigned — compiler confirms
    threshold = 300000;  // IF added: ERROR AT LAMBDA: "must be final or effectively final"
    Lambda captures threshold (Recommended) 

  ═══ IDENTICAL BEHAVIOR ═══

  Bytecode: SAME for both
  Captured value: SAME (copy of 200000)
  Lambda behavior: SAME
  Performance: SAME

  ═══ WHEN TO USE WHICH ═══

  explicit final:                      effectively final:
  ├─ Method parameters (document)      ├─ Simple local variables
  ├─ Configuration constants           ├─ Obviously never reassigned
  ├─ Loop variables captured by lambda ├─ Reduces code noise
  └─ Team coding standard requires     └─ Most common in practice
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
There is NO behavioral difference between an effectively final variable and an explicitly final variable for lambda capture. The compiler treats them identically — both produce the same bytecode, both capture the same value copy, and both prevent reassignment. The only difference is where the compile error appears: explicitly `final` catches reassignment at the assignment line ("cannot assign to final variable"), effectively final catches it at the lambda line ("must be final or effectively final").

In my demo service, `final BigDecimal threshold = 200000` and `BigDecimal threshold = 200000` (never reassigned) produce IDENTICAL filter results — both capture 200000, both filter the same 3 trades. The `final` keyword is purely documentation: "I promise this won't change." Effectively final relies on the compiler to verify the same promise without the keyword.

When to prefer explicit `final`: method parameters (documents the contract), configuration constants, and loop variables captured by lambdas in executor.submit. When effectively final is sufficient: simple local variables that are obviously never reassigned — adding `final` to every local variable adds noise without value. Historically, Java 7 anonymous inner classes required explicit `final`. Java 8 lambdas relaxed this to accept effectively final — making `final` optional for lambda capture.
